topic: Focus on the solution. Protect the patient’s dignity.
title: Focus on the solution. Protect the patient’s dignity.
dek: The Redo Room shows how dental work that did not turn out right can be corrected, without shaming the patient or the dentist who came before.

body.p: Some cosmetic dental work does not turn out the way the patient hoped. Veneers can look bulky or too white, shades can stop matching, bonding can chip, and a smile line can end up flat. The Redo Room is our series about fixing those problems. It has two rules: focus on the solution, and protect the patient's dignity.

Every redo starts with understanding why the first result did not work. Was it the shape, the color, the thickness, the gums or the bite? A careful dentist examines the existing work, takes photos and scans, and explains what can realistically be improved before removing anything. The articles in this series walk through how common problems are usually assessed and corrected.

People who need a redo often feel embarrassed, or worry they made a bad decision. They did not. We never feature a patient without written consent, we never mock anyone's teeth, and we do not criticize the dentist who did the earlier work. The point is to show what is possible, so people in the same situation know they have options.

body.h: What to ask if you need a redo

ul: What exactly is wrong with my current work, and why?
Can it be repaired, or does it need to be replaced?
Will removing it affect my natural teeth?
Can I see a preview of the new design first?
What does the warranty cover this time?

body.p: Corrective work can be more complex than a first-time treatment, so it is worth taking time to find a dentist who does it regularly and explains the plan clearly.

title: Replacing bulky veneers: how thick work gets slimmed down
dek: Bulky veneers can often be redone with thinner, better-shaped ones, but it starts with a careful exam of the teeth and gums underneath.

body.p: Bulky veneers are one of the most common reasons people look for a redo. The teeth look too big, too far forward or too thick. Lips can feel pushed out, and the gums along the edges may be irritated. The good news is that they can often be replaced with a slimmer, more natural design. The honest news is that a redo needs more care than the first round, not less.

Veneers are thin shells bonded to the front of the teeth. They look bulky when material is added on top of teeth without enough planning for where the final surface should sit. Common causes include placing veneers over teeth that were crowded or tipped forward, making shades very light so thicker material was needed to hide darker teeth, or choosing large shapes without testing them first. Thick edges near the gums can also make cleaning harder, which may lead to puffy or bleeding tissue.

body.h: How a redo is typically assessed

ul: Photos, video and a smile analysis to see how the teeth relate to the lips, face and gums.
An exam of the gums and bite, plus X-rays to check the teeth under the veneers for decay or other problems.
A review of how much enamel likely remains. Porcelain veneers require removing some enamel, and older work may have removed more.
A design preview, often a digital plan and a temporary mock-up, to show the slimmer result before anything is removed.

body.p: The old veneers are carefully removed, usually by grinding them away, and the underlying teeth are checked and cleaned up. The dentist then shapes the teeth to support thinner restorations where possible. Planning literature for conservative veneers emphasizes keeping preparation within enamel when possible because bonding to enamel is more reliable. Temporaries let you test the new size and shape while the lab makes the final veneers.

Sometimes slimmer veneers are only possible if teeth are first moved back into a better position with orthodontics, or if gum levels are adjusted. That can add time, but it can also mean less additional tooth reduction. Veneers commonly last 10 to 15 years with good care, so the redo is a long-term decision.

At a consultation, ask what is under your current veneers, how much enamel remains and whether a mock-up can show you the slimmer design first. Ask about every option, including orthodontics before veneers. Every mouth is different, so the plan depends on an in-person exam.

title: Fixing mismatched shades: bringing one smile back to one color
dek: When restorations and natural teeth no longer match, the fix depends on what changed and what can still change color.

body.p: A shade mismatch is easy to spot and frustrating to live with. One crown is grayer than the rest. Veneers look whiter than the lower teeth. Old bonding has yellowed while the teeth around it stayed light. The right fix depends on a simple question: which parts can still change color, and which cannot?

ul: Natural teeth change. They can darken with age, stain from coffee, tea, wine or tobacco, or lighten with whitening.
Restorations do not respond to whitening. The ADA notes that whitening will not work on caps, veneers, crowns or fillings.
Composite bonding can stain or dull over time, while porcelain is generally more color-stable.
The original shade may have been chosen in poor light, on dried-out teeth, or without considering the lower teeth.
Technical issues during finishing or bonding can also affect color. A clinical survey of porcelain veneers found color change was the most common type of failure it recorded.

body.p: A dentist starts by mapping what is natural and what is restored, and photographs the teeth in consistent light. Shade-selection guidance recommends balanced daylight or color-corrected light, neutral surroundings, no lipstick and moist teeth, since teeth that dry out look lighter. Many offices combine visual shade guides with digital measurement. The dentist also checks whether discoloration is surface staining, aging, or a darkening tooth that may need its own evaluation.

ul: Whitening natural teeth up to match brighter restorations, when the restorations are otherwise sound.
Polishing or replacing stained bonding to match the surrounding teeth.
Replacing a single crown or veneer that stands out, with the new shade chosen against the teeth around it.
Replacing a group of restorations together when several are mismatched, so they can be designed as a set.

body.p: The order matters. If whitening is part of the plan, it usually comes first, and new restorations are matched after the color settles. Matching a single front tooth to its natural neighbor is one of the hardest jobs in cosmetic dentistry, and it may take more than one try-in to get right.

At a consultation, ask which of your teeth are restored, whether whitening is part of the plan and in what light the new shade will be chosen. Ask to see the shade in your mouth before it is final. Your teeth decide the options, so it starts with an exam.

title: Correcting a flat smile line: restoring the curve
dek: A flat smile line can make a smile look older or artificial, and correcting it means re-planning the edges, the gums and sometimes the bite together.

body.p: A flat smile line is one of the quieter giveaways in cosmetic dentistry. The upper front teeth end in a straight horizontal line rather than a gentle curve. Even when the color is good, the smile can look older, harder or more artificial. Correcting it is less about adding length and more about redesigning the edge.

body.h: What a flat smile line is

body.p: When you smile, the tips of the upper teeth form what dentists call the smile arc. In a consonant arc, that curve runs roughly parallel to the inner curve of the lower lip. In a flat arc, the edges run straighter than the lip. Smile-design literature notes that the arc tends to flatten with age, and that it can also flatten because of tooth position or treatment choices. In cosmetic work, a flat line often comes from veneers or crowns with every edge set to the same length.

ul: Photos and video of your natural smile and speech, taken level with your mouth.
How much tooth shows at rest and when smiling, and how the edges sit against the lower lip.
The bite, including wear, grinding and how the front teeth guide the jaw.
Gum levels, since uneven or low gums can limit how the edges can be reshaped.
Whether the existing teeth or restorations can be adjusted or need replacement.

body.p: A plan often starts with a digital design and a temporary mock-up, so you can see and feel the new curve before anything permanent is done. The two central incisors are usually set slightly longer than the laterals, and the edges step up gently toward the sides. Depending on the cause, correction may involve reshaping or replacing veneers or crowns, adding bonding, orthodontics to change tooth position, or gum procedures to balance the frame. Published cases describe combining veneers with surgical crown lengthening to correct vertical discrepancies, using a design that plans teeth and gums together.
The bite is part of the decision. Edges that look good but collide with the lower teeth are more likely to chip, so the new curve has to be tested for speech and function as well as looks.

At a consultation, ask how your edges relate to your lower lip, whether a mock-up can show the new curve and whether your bite or gums need attention first. Your lip line, bite and gums set the possibilities, so an in-person exam is essential.

title: Repairing chipped bonding: when to patch and when to redo
dek: Small chips in composite bonding can often be repaired in a single visit, while widespread staining, wear or decay may call for replacement.

body.p: Composite bonding is one of the most flexible tools in cosmetic dentistry. It is also one of the easiest to chip. The upside is that bonding is usually easy to repair too. Many chips can be smoothed or rebuilt without starting over. Knowing when a repair makes sense, and when it does not, saves time and tooth structure.

Bonding uses tooth-colored composite resin shaped directly on the tooth. Cleveland Clinic notes it typically lasts about three to 10 years before it needs touch-ups or replacement, depending on habits and how many teeth are involved. Common causes of chips include biting nails, chewing pens or ice, opening packages with teeth, grinding at night and edges that take too much force from the bite. Composite is also less stain-resistant than porcelain, so older bonding may dull or discolor.

body.h: How a chip is typically assessed

ul: Size and location of the chip, and whether it is in the material or the tooth itself.
Whether the rest of the bonding is sound, with tight edges and no staining at the margins.
Any signs of decay underneath, which change the plan.
The bite and habits that may have caused the chip, so it does not happen again.
How well the existing color and surface still match the neighboring teeth.

body.p: For a small, localized chip on otherwise healthy bonding, repair is often the conservative choice. The dentist roughens and cleans the area, adds new composite, shapes it and polishes it to blend. A recent systematic review of partially fractured composite restorations found repairs offered comparable longevity to full replacement while preserving tooth structure, though the authors noted the evidence base is limited.

Replacement makes more sense when bonding is extensively stained, worn or rough, when the color no longer matches, when there is decay underneath, or when chips keep returning because the design or bite is wrong. In some cases, a dentist may discuss porcelain veneers or other options if bonding keeps failing in the same spot.

ul: Call your dentist if a bonded tooth has a sharp edge or your bite feels off.
Avoid using your teeth as tools, and ask about a night guard if you grind.
Keep regular cleanings, where bonding can be checked and polished.

body.p: At a consultation, ask whether your chip can be repaired or needs a redo, what caused it and how to prevent it next time. Only an exam can tell whether the bonding and the tooth beneath it are sound.
